items.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019
items.q: He wrote a book back then called The Agony of Modern Music. The whole point of the book was the vital spirit that used to be in Beethoven and Mozart and those guys is no longer in classical music, it is now in jazz.

ctx.x: What did you learn from Dizzy?

Oh man. How long a tape is that? The concept — Dizzy changed music organically. I don’t know if you remember Henry Pleasants. He was the classical music critic for the New York Times. He wrote a book back then called The Agony of Modern Music. The whole point of the book was the vital spirit that used to be in Beethoven and Mozart and those guys is no longer in classical music, it is now in jazz. And he specifically pointed out Dizzy and Charlie Parker. He said they represented the first organic change in music…

“Did you just hear that?” It didn’t affect his playing. He couldn’t hit a high F or something like that. But what I learned from Dizzy is, I have a four DVD series out called The Rhythmic Nature of Jazz that actually, in the order that I learned everything from Dizzy is the whole concept is on those four DVDs. And so they’re progressive. You have to learn this first, then the second DVD. But everything I learned from Dizzy is on those DVDs, in the order that I learned them. It’s very deep. Dizzy’s stuff was very,…
